title: The specialists lost. The discounters did not.
lede: In 2001 KB had about 6% of a $30 billion U.S. toy retail market.[^15] Every company on this page that sold mainly toys has since gone through bankruptcy. The two that sold toys as one aisle among many are still open.

blocks.title: Who sold America its toys, and what became of them
blocks.subtitle: One figure for each, from the period when KB was failing.

items.name: KB Toys
items.text: Share of U.S. toy retail in 2001, as reported by the Associated Press, and an analyst’s estimate in 2008.[^15][^23] Liquidated in 2008–09.

items.name: Walmart
items.text: Share of the U.S. toy market in 2007, a consultant’s estimate. By then it was the top U.S. toy seller.[^22]

items.name: Toys “R” Us
items.text: Taken private for $6.6B in 2005 by a group that included Bain Capital.[^21] Said in March 2018 that it expected to close all 735 U.S. stores.[^31]

items.name: FAO Inc.
items.text: The parent of FAO Schwarz, Zany Brainy and The Right Start filed for Chapter 11 about a month before KB.[^18]

items.name: eToys
items.text: The web toy retailer, founded in 1996, never made a profit. KB bought part of its inventory for about $5.4M.[^16]

blocks.source: Figures as cited. The share figures are press-reported estimates and are not on a common basis. Walmart and Target are still operating (general knowledge).

blocks.title: What each side had
rows: About 3,315 selling sq ft in an enclosed mall[^4]

They were at the mall already[^21]

blocks.text: If you ask why are toy retailers hurting, it's because their offering was less and less differentiated from a discounter's.
blocks.who: Jacques Roizen, Alvarez & Marsal, to USA Today, January 14, 2004[^18]
